name: Apple Pay and Private Click Measurement flags
plain: Safari-only flags: Apple Pay availability and ad attribution support.
meaning: ApplePaySession.canMakePayments reveals whether Apple Pay is set up on the device (a financial hint) and PCM support marks Safari. Both are tested by FingerprintJS.

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

fields.name: applePayState
fields.range: -1 unavailable, 0 available no card, 1 card set up

limits.headline: Can check if Apple Pay is set up and if you use Safari
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads
can: Tell if Apple Pay can be used on your device
Tell if ad attribution features exist, which marks the browser as Safari
Add both as clues to a device profile
cannot: See your cards or card numbers
Start a payment without you confirming it
Work in Chrome, Edge or Firefox
limits.differs: Only Safari on iPhone and Mac has these checks. Chrome, Edge and Firefox do not.

story.what_it_is: Safari tells a site whether Apple Pay works on this device and whether ad click measurement is supported.

marketing.name: Apple Pay on the Web
marketing.pitch: Apple describes a fast and private way to check out on websites with Touch ID or Face ID.

marketing.name: Private Click Measurement
marketing.pitch: WebKit explains a way to measure ad conversions while keeping people's browsing private.

story.for_you: You see an Apple Pay button on a checkout only when your device can use it. The site learns you are on Safari, and may use a private ad click report that does not identify you.
story.for_makers: Shops show the button only to people who can use it, which lifts checkout rates. Advertisers use the private measurement to learn which ads led to a sale without tracking people across sites. Trackers also use the flags to confirm a real Apple device.

use_cases.example: A retailer shows the Apple Pay button only on devices where it works, so checkout takes one tap.
A payment provider checks Apple Pay readiness before it offers the option.
An advertiser measures how many Safari users bought after clicking an ad, with a coarse and private report.
A news site offers a quick Apple Pay subscription button to Safari readers.
A food ordering site shows Apple Pay first on iPhone, so you can pay in a few seconds.
A fraud engine checks that the claimed iPhone really supports Apple Pay, to catch fake devices.
A booking site shows Apple Pay on Safari so you can finish a booking on your phone quickly.

history.change: Payment capabilities readback restricted for known fingerprinters
